lesson.title: Plaintext and Exposed: Why Telnet Gave Way to SSH
lesson.summary: Telnet provides remote terminal access over TCP but sends everything, including passwords, in unencrypted plaintext, a flaw serious enough that it has been almost entirely replaced by SSH for actual remote login.
lesson.body:
Telnet is an application layer protocol, running over TCP, that lets a user log into a remote machine and interact with it as though sitting at its terminal, typing commands and seeing their output, over the network rather than physically at the machine. For a long time this was simply how remote administration worked: connect over TCP, usually to port 23, authenticate, and get a shell on a distant computer.

The problem with Telnet, and the reason it has been almost entirely retired for this purpose, is that it applies no encryption whatsoever. Every keystroke sent from the client to the server, and every character sent back, travels across the network as plain, readable text. That includes the username and password typed in to log in. Anyone positioned to observe traffic along the path between the client and the server, whether that means another device on the same local network, a compromised router somewhere along the route, or anyone running a packet capture on shared Wi-Fi, can simply read the login credentials and everything typed during the session directly out of the traffic, with no need to break any encryption because there is none to break.

This is exactly the gap that SSH was built to close. SSH provides the same basic capability, a remote terminal session over the network, but encrypts the entire session from the moment the connection is established, so that even someone capturing every packet sees only ciphertext, not commands or passwords. Once SSH became widely available, there was very little reason to keep using Telnet for remote administration, and it has been superseded by SSH almost everywhere a real login to a remote system is needed, especially anywhere that connection might cross a network the administrator does not fully control.

Telnet has not disappeared entirely, though its remaining use is quite different from its original purpose. Because a Telnet client is really just a simple way to open a raw TCP connection to a given host and port and exchange text over it, administrators still sometimes use the telnet command as a quick diagnostic tool, for example to check whether a particular port on a server is open and accepting connections, or even to manually type a few commands from a text based protocol, like the SMTP commands covered earlier, directly into the connection to see how a server responds. That diagnostic use survives precisely because it does not involve logging into anything or sending sensitive credentials, which is the part of Telnet's original job that plaintext transmission made unacceptable.
